query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn, dynamic mechanical behavior across temperature and strain‐rate regimes is controlled by an elastic strain‐induced amorphization mechanism that limits conventional dislocation nucleation, thereby sustaining a strength–ductility balance.
generation.material_initial_state: Solidified, single‐phase, Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy with a homogeneous chemical distribution and minimal pre‐existing defects.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to uniaxial mechanical loading (tension or compression) under controlled temperature (ranging from cryogenic to elevated) and strain-rate conditions.
generation.conditions: Tests must maintain the as‐solidified microstructure (i.e. no additional phase separation or second phases introduced) and apply strains up to and beyond the ~10% elastic strain threshold reported in similar HEAs.
generation.structural_mediator: Local atomic disorder manifested as elastic strain‐induced amorphous regions at high elastic strains.
generation.mechanism: Under dynamic loading, the inherent local chemical inhomogeneities in the Co‐free system depress conventional dislocation nucleation. Instead, when the applied elastic strain nears ~10%, the lattice locally becomes amorphous, effectively softening dislocation activity and modulating strain hardening. This amorphization onset varies with temperature and strain rate, thus governing the balance between strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: At lower temperatures or under higher strain rates, the threshold strain for amorphization may shift, leading to observable changes in yield stress and hardening rate. In situ microscopy (e.g., TEM) should reveal localized regions of loss of lattice order (incipient amorphization) coinciding with a decline in dislocation density, correlating with the mechanical response.
generation.baseline: Mechanical responses (stress–strain behavior) and microstructural features (lattice order via diffraction or TEM) measured at room temperature and moderate strain rates, where the amorphization onset and its effects are characterized.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloys that are single‐phase and lack significant second-phase precipitates or large-scale microstructural heterogeneities. At extreme conditions (very high temperatures or strain rates), additional mechanisms (e.g., twinning or phase transformations) may become significant.
generation.uncertainty: Exact strain thresholds for the amorphization onset and its quantitative contribution relative to conventional dislocation or twinning mechanisms remain uncertain; further in situ observations are necessary to firmly establish the interplay.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare as-solidified, homogeneous Co-free FeNiCrMn samples. Conduct in situ uniaxial tensile or compressive tests under a series of controlled temperatures (cryogenic, room temperature, and elevated) and strain rates. Use TEM with diffraction capabilities to monitor the microstructural evolution, focusing on the appearance of amorphization and changes in dislocation densities near strains of ~10%.
measurements: Stress–strain curves for yield strength and strain-hardening behavior
TEM imaging and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED) to detect loss of lattice order
Quantitative analysis of dislocation density before and after the predicted strain threshold
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under the tested conditions there is no evidence of an abrupt local loss of crystalline order (i.e., no onset of amorphization) at the predicted elastic strain levels, or if variations in dynamic mechanical properties can be fully explained by alternative mechanisms (e.g., increased dislocation activity or twinning without amorphization), the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Elastic strain-induced amorphization in high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractElastic stability is the basis for understanding structural responses to external stimuli in crystalline solids, including melting, incipient plasticity and fracture. In this work, elastic stability is investigated in a series of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) using in situ mechanical tests and atomic-resolution characterization in transmission electron microscopy. Under tensile loading, the HEA lattices are observed to undergo a sudden loss of ordering as the elastic strain reached ∽ 10%. Such elastic strain-induced amorphization stands in intrinsic contrast to previously reported dislocation-mediated elastic instability and defect accumulation-mediated amorphization, introducing a form of elastic instability. Together with the first principle calculations and atomic-resolution chemical mapping, we identify that the elastic strain-induced amorphization is closely related to the depressed dislocation nucleation due to the local atomic environment inhomogeneity of HEAs.
